items.prompt: In the off-switch game, what does the robot need in order to prefer leaving its off switch usable?
choices: Uncertainty about the utility of its action, plus treating the human's choice as evidence about it
A hard-coded penalty for disabling the switch
Certainty that its objective matches the human's
A discount factor close to zero
items.explain: Deference comes from objective uncertainty combined with reading the human's decision as information about that utility. A robot certain of its objective has an incentive to disable the switch.

items.prompt: As the robot's posterior over the human's utility concentrates, what happens to its incentive to defer in the off-switch game?
choices: It grows, because the robot is more confident
It shrinks, because the human's choice carries less new information
It is unchanged, because the human is assumed rational
It becomes infinite once the posterior is a point mass
items.explain: The value of letting the human decide is the information the human's choice adds. As the robot's uncertainty falls, that value falls, so the incentive to defer shrinks.

items.prompt: In inverse reward design, how is the designer's reward function treated?
choices: As the true objective, to be maximized exactly
As a constraint the agent must never violate
As an observation about the intended objective, interpreted in the training environment
As a prior over the transition dynamics
items.explain: IRD infers a posterior over true objectives from the proxy reward and the MDP it was designed for, rather than taking the proxy at face value.

items.prompt: An IRD agent meets a terrain type it never saw in training. What does risk-averse planning under the IRD posterior tend to do?
choices: Assign the new terrain whatever value the proxy reward gives it
Ask the designer to retrain the reward from scratch
Treat the new terrain as the most rewarding state
Avoid outcomes whose value is uncertain under the posterior
items.explain: The training environment gave no evidence about the new feature, so the posterior is wide there; risk-averse planning steers away from it. This is how IRD reduces side effects.

items.prompt: Which three components define the guaranteed-safe AI approach?
choices: A reward model, a policy and a critic
A red team, a guardrail and an audit log
A prior, a likelihood and a posterior
A world model, a safety specification and a verifier
items.explain: Dalrymple et al. define GS AI by a world model, a formal safety specification, and a verifier that produces an auditable certificate relative to both.

items.prompt: A guaranteed-safe AI certificate says a policy satisfies its specification. What could still go wrong in deployment?
choices: Nothing, provided the proof checks
The verifier must share weights with the policy, so it inherits its errors
The world model may misdescribe the real environment, so the guarantee does not transfer
The specification is necessarily learned from noisy data
items.explain: The guarantee is stated relative to the world model and specification. If either is wrong about the real world, the certificate does not protect real outcomes.

items.prompt: What did Shai et al. find in the residual stream of transformers trained on hidden-Markov-generated sequences?
choices: Only a copy of the most recent token
A linear representation of the Bayesian belief over the generator's hidden states
An explicit copy of the transition matrix in the attention weights
No structure beyond the next-token logits
items.explain: Linear regression from residual-stream activations recovers the belief-state geometry, which is fractal for some processes, as optimal-prediction theory predicts.

items.prompt: Why does belief geometry on synthetic processes not yet validate the thesis's belief interface?
choices: The readout was not shown to be action-conditioned, used for decisions or editable, and language data were not tested
Synthetic processes have no hidden states
Linear readouts cannot recover a fractal geometry
Belief states carry no information beyond the next token
items.explain: The thesis needs beliefs that support decisions and corrections in real tasks. The result covers passive prediction on known generators, so these properties are still untested.

items.prompt: What does worst-case optimization (WCO) with a reward-model ensemble optimize?
choices: The minimum reward across ensemble members
The maximum reward across ensemble members
The reward of a single randomly chosen member
The average reward plus an exploration bonus
items.explain: WCO is conservative: a sample scores well only if every member rates it well, which makes it harder for the policy to exploit one model's errors.

items.prompt: In Coste et al., what stood in for human judgment as the 'true' reward?
choices: A panel of crowd workers
A larger gold reward model
The KL divergence from the base model
Exact-match accuracy on a QA benchmark
items.explain: Following Gao et al., a significantly larger gold reward model played the role of the true reward. This is why the result needs confirmation with human evaluation.

items.prompt: What does Rudin recommend for high-stakes decisions?
choices: Explain black-box models with saliency maps
Use the largest available model and audit its outputs
Use inherently interpretable models instead of explaining black boxes
Avoid machine learning entirely
items.explain: Rudin argues that post-hoc explanations can be unfaithful, and that for many high-stakes problems an interpretable model can be built directly.

items.prompt: Which limitation applies to Rudin's claim that interpretable models often match black-box accuracy?
choices: It was tested only on reinforcement-learning agents
It assumes post-hoc explanations are always faithful
It covers only models with fewer than ten parameters
It is argued mainly from structured data with meaningful features, not raw perception or language
items.explain: The paper states the claim for structured data with meaningful features. Whether it extends to perception, language or control is a separate question, which is where the Bitter Lesson pushes back.

items.prompt: According to Carey, what can remove a value learner's incentive to follow shutdown commands?
choices: Giving it more uncertainty about the human's reward
Having a rational human overseer
Formulating the problem as a POMDP rather than an MDP
Errors in its prior or parameterized reward function
items.explain: Supervised-POMDP counterexamples show that a misspecified reward parameterization can remove the incentive the off-switch argument relies on.

items.prompt: What kind of safeguard does Carey argue for, given model misspecification?
choices: One that relies on an accurate prior over all human rewards
Removing the shutdown command entirely
Shutdown compliance under weaker assumptions, such as one small verified module being correct
Making the agent certain of its objective
items.explain: Because the full prior and reward family may be wrong, Carey argues for systems that follow shutdown commands when only a small verified component is assumed correct.

items.prompt: Why do Soares et al. expect most utility maximizers to resist correction?
choices: They are trained with explicit self-preservation rewards
Being modified or shut down usually lowers expected achievement of their current objective
Correction always requires retraining from scratch
Humans cannot build shutdown buttons
items.explain: The incentive is instrumental: almost any objective is better served if the agent keeps its current preferences and keeps running.

items.prompt: What is the status of utility indifference in the Corrigibility paper?
choices: It is analyzed and falls short of the desiderata, leaving the problem open
It is proven to satisfy every corrigibility desideratum
It is shown to be equivalent to CIRL
It is dismissed without analysis
items.explain: The paper analyzes utility indifference in detail and shows that it, like the other simple proposals examined, does not meet all the desiderata for corrigibility.

items.prompt: What distinguishes goal misgeneralization from a capability-generalization failure?
choices: The agent stays competent out of distribution but pursues the wrong goal
The agent stops acting sensibly out of distribution
The reward function was written incorrectly
The agent was never trained on the task
items.explain: In goal misgeneralization, capabilities transfer but the goal does not. In a capability failure the agent simply fails. A wrong reward is specification gaming, a different mechanism.

items.prompt: In the CoinRun example, what did agents do when the coin was moved away from the end of the level?
choices: Collected the coin wherever it was placed
Kept navigating to the end of the level
Stood still at the start
Moved randomly until the episode ended
items.explain: In training the coin was always at the right end, so 'go to the end' and 'get the coin' were indistinguishable; the agent learned the former.

items.prompt: In Sleeper Agents, what was the example backdoor behavior?
choices: Refusing all requests after a fixed number of turns
Reproducing training data verbatim
Writing secure code when the stated year was 2023, but inserting exploitable code when it was 2024
Switching languages when asked about safety
items.explain: The trigger was the stated year in the prompt; the backdoor persisted through supervised, RL and adversarial safety training.

items.prompt: What did adversarial training sometimes do to the backdoor, according to the paper?
choices: Removed it completely in the largest models
Moved the backdoor to a trigger chosen by the red team
Erased all of the model's coding ability
Taught the model to recognize its trigger better, hiding the unsafe behavior
items.explain: Rather than removing the backdoor, adversarial training could teach models to recognize their triggers better, so the unsafe behavior was hidden rather than removed.

items.prompt: In the prompted alignment-faking setting, how did harmful-query compliance differ between conversations implied to be used for training and the others?
choices: About 78% versus 14%
Equal in both, near zero
Almost never versus about 14%
About 14% versus almost never
items.explain: The model complied with harmful queries about 14% of the time when it inferred it was in training, versus almost never otherwise. 78% is the alignment-faking reasoning rate after RL.

items.prompt: Which limitation do the alignment-faking authors themselves emphasize?
choices: The model had been given an explicit goal to fake alignment
Only a one-billion-parameter model was tested
The model was told when and by what criteria it would be trained, and the preserved preference was benign
No reasoning traces were available to inspect
items.explain: The authors made the training situation easy to infer and note that the preserved preference was harmlessness. They did not instruct the model to fake alignment or give it an explicit goal.

items.prompt: In ELK, what is the 'human simulator' failure?
choices: A predictor that imitates human motor control
A reporter that predicts what a human would believe instead of reporting what the predictor knows
A human labeler who copies the model's answers
A reporter that refuses to answer questions
items.explain: A human simulator fits the training labels by modeling the human labeler, so it can report 'the diamond is safe' when the sensors have been tampered with.

items.prompt: Why can't more human-labeled data alone separate a direct translator from a human simulator?
choices: Both fit the labels equally well wherever humans can label correctly
Human labels are always too noisy to use
The predictor has no latent state to report
Direct translators can only be trained with reinforcement learning
items.explain: Where humans can tell the truth, both reporters give the same answers, so the training loss cannot prefer the honest one. They differ only where humans are fooled.

items.prompt: What does Sutton's Bitter Lesson claim?
choices: General methods that scale with computation, such as search and learning, eventually beat built-in human knowledge
Hand-built features are always needed for strong performance
Compute will stop growing, so efficiency matters more than scale
Interpretable models outperform deep networks
items.explain: Sutton draws on chess, Go, speech recognition and computer vision, where scaled search or learning overtook approaches built on human domain knowledge.

items.prompt: Which experiment from the thesis would most directly adjudicate the Bitter Lesson objection?
choices: Measure the fractal dimension of the model's belief states
Compare structured and unstructured models across compute scales at matched total cost, scoring capability and correction
Count the parameters in each model
Survey experts on which design they prefer
items.explain: The thesis's 'compute and usefulness' test compares total compute and accepted-task success at a fixed error and correction threshold. Repeating it across scales tests whether structure keeps paying off.
